title: Berkshire 1984 letter: buybacks, dividend policy, bonds as businesses, and dominant franchises
summary: Buffett explains when retained earnings are justified, why buybacks below intrinsic value reveal pro-owner managers, and why he values even bonds like businesses. He also covers dominant newspaper economics, owner-style incentives for unconventional bets, and how insolvent insurers distort the industry.

principles.text: Retain earnings only if each retained dollar creates at least a dollar of market value for owners.
principles.quote: for every dollar retained by the corporation, at least one dollar of market value will be created for owners.

principles.text: Buybacks well below intrinsic value are the surest way to create value, and beat most acquisitions.
principles.quote: When companies purchase their own stock, they often find it easy to get $2 of present value for $1.

principles.text: A manager who ignores sensible buybacks reveals his true priorities, whatever he says publicly.
principles.quote: A manager who consistently turns his back on repurchases, when these clearly are in the interests of owners, reveals more than he knows of his motivations.

principles.text: Evaluate every investment, even bonds, as you would buying a business.
principles.quote: Investment is most intelligent when it is most businesslike.

principles.text: Dominant newspapers earn excellent returns regardless of quality, so management must impose its own standards.
principles.quote: While first-class newspapers make excellent profits, the profits of third-rate papers are as good or better - as long as either class of paper is dominant within its community.

principles.text: Insolvent insurers keep writing business at any price because cash arrives before losses are paid.
principles.quote: In most businesses, of course, insolvent companies run out of cash. Insurance is different: you can be broke but flush.
